_source.displaydescription:
The Caitya is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) and is part of a group of four caityas and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala, all of which are aligned in a north-south direction. The area surrounding the caitya is paved with black flagstones and has been encroached upon by some of the building materials used for the reconstruction of the Mandira.

Generally, caityas follow the pattern of placing statues of Akṣobhya to the east, Amoghasiddhi to the north, Amitābha to the west and Ratnasambhava to the south. However, this Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya displays statues of Vairocana to the east, Mañjuśrī to the north, Vajrasattva to the west and Amitābha to the south.

This monument was constructed in 1983, and its anniversary worship is performed on the full moon day of Vaiśākha. Tradition dictates that an umbrella be placed on top of the caitya on the full moon day of Āśvina.
_source.displayname: Dharmadhātujinālaya Caitya (1983 CE) || धर्मधातुजिनालय चैत्य || BUN0013

Kularatna Vihāra is a branch of Cikã Bahī. It can be accessed via a narrow alley that runs under a residential building on the way to Cyāsal from Bhelāchẽ. The west-facing god house has a carved door, but lacks a toraṇa. There are no stone lions in front of the door and even the panels of the door are not fixed in place. A stone image of Akṣobhya can be found inside the sanctum - this small image is a replacement of the previous one, which was stolen in the 1960s. To the left of Akṣobhya, one can see a stone statue of a six-armed Mañjuvajra. He holds a sword and an arrow in his two right hands and performs varada with the third one. His three left hands can be seen holding a book of the Prajñāpāramitā, a lotus flower and a bow. Tārā sits to the right of Akṣobhya, and is performing varada and abhaya and holding lotus stalks in her two hands. To the left of Tārā, one can find a terracotta image of Red Matsyendranātha. His body is covered with a red cloth. According to local informants, this particular image was installed around 40 years ago.

This vihāra is attached to the eastern boundary wall of a courtyard that measures 23 m x 8 m. The courtyard can be accessed through an opening on its western wall, which also contains images of Bhīmasena and Gaṇeśa. The building is a simple one-storey structure, and its back wall shares the courtyard's boundary wall. The three other sides are partitioned with timber lattice work. The main door is to the west, and is a swing door with metal vertical rails. The building is raised above the level of the courtyard in that it sits on a stone plinth of 1.8 m x 2.4 m.

It appears that the plinth was recently covered with a concrete flat slab that is supported by brick piers on the western side. The roof has a stūpa finial that has been built with bricks on cement mortar. In front of the sanctum, one can find a small dharmadhātu maṇḍala. The western residential building in front of the vihāra has some remaining traditional wall paintings on the first floor level, though these are rapidly deteriorating.

No inscription could be found to provide information about the establishment of this vihāra. However, Gellner (1987, 405) mentions that the nearby Bhaiṣajya Vihāra was established by Jīvanṛsiṃha in 1878 (NS 998). He claims that his eldest son established this Kularatna Vihāra some years later.

The area around the Kumbheśhvara temple, north of Patan is called Kobāhaḥ. There are numerous references to Ko Bāhāḥ or Ko Vihāra situated in this area dating back to the fourteen century (Locke 1985, 128). Dozens of late-Malla period inscriptions also use the word Kobāhā to describe the area. These references assert that there was a big monastery called Ko Bāhāḥ in this area. However, Locke (ibid.) doubts that this small Bāhāḥ is identical with the historical Ko Bāhāḥ and assumes that this Bāhāḥ was a branch of Kvā Bāhāḥ. At present, the Bāhāḥ, also called Ituṅ Bāhāḥ, is very small and looks like a śākhāvihāra (branch monastery). It is possible that the Ituṅ Bāhāḥ located in the Ko Bāhāḥ area, was later associated with the name.

A pair of stone lions sitting on the sides of the entrance guard the Bāhāḥ. The Carved wooden door is surmounted by a toraṇa with the images of Triratna. First-floor façade has a three-bayed window. Inside the sanctum sanctorum lies a metal statue of Akṣobhya. There was a statue of Cakrasamvara on the first floor, however it is lost. Now only two small statues of Kumārī and Bhairava are lying there. Besides, there is a small wooden caitya. A vajradhātu caitya stands in the courtyard.  Locke (ibid.) and Pruscha (1975, 168) mention that there are two stone caityas in the Bāhāḥ complex, but these are not found.

No historical record is available to date the Bāhāḥ. Four families associated with the Guji Bāhāḥ Saṅgha were performing the daily and other worships in the Bāhāḥ who around 100 years before got the authority. Since 2000 CE, they have also left the area and their duty. They handed over the authority to a Śākya family living in a house attached to the Bāhāḥ complex. At present, the family is taking care of the Bāhāḥ and performing the worships. Earlier, the annual worship of this Baha was performed in the month of Karttika, but the tradition discontinued about 25 years ago.

Sum Bāhāḥ is a branch of Jyo Bāhāḥ (LAL1770). It has a two-storied shrine (dyaḥchẽ) which faces west. The roof of the dyaḥchẽ which is supported by the plain struts was originally tiled with the jhĩgaṭīs slates, but it is now covered with the corrugated pewter sheets.[1] The first floor has a trikhā-window flanked by tiki-windows. Also, a sacred place for Bāhāḥ’s esoteric deity (āgama) is on the second floor. The sanctum (garbhagṛha) of the dyaḥchẽ is on its first floor.

Previously, a wooden toraṇa on which the images of Akṣobhya (in the middle), and Prañāpāramitā and Lokeśvara (to the right and left of Akṣobhya) was kept above the main door to the dyaḥchẽ (cf. Locke 1985, 77). However, this disappeared or most probably got stolen sometime before 1985 CE. A stone statue of Akṣobhya, flanked by the Sūrya (the god Sun) statue, has been enshrined in the sanctum sanctorum as the Bāhāḥ’s kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ.[2] A Dharmadhātujinālaṃkṛta Caitya and Dharmadhātu Maṇdala (erected in NS 984, i.e. 1864 CE and NS 1057, i.e. 1937 CE, respectively) are established in the Bāhā’s courtyard.[3]

Although no documented evidence is so far found to date the Bāhāḥ’s initial construction, a copy of the document reporting the various events suggests that it must have been built before 1536 CE.[4] When King Raṇa Bahādura (r. 1777-1799) confiscated guṭhī land in the Kathmandu Valley, large portion of guṭhī land of this Bāhāḥ, too, was confiscated.[5] Previously, four Śākya families were involved to perform the daily rituals having endowed two ropanīs of land (from each family). However, only the family of Puṇyarāja Śākya (Śukrarāja Śākya) carries out this task now. The Yogāmbara worship which used to take place every year (on the 10th of the dark fortnight of Māgha) does not take place anymore in the Bāhāḥ. The dyaḥchẽ was severely damaged during the 2015 earthquakes. The Lalitpur Metropolitan Office has recently allocated 5 lakhs to renovate it.

Footnotes

  1. ^ This dyaḥchẽ has no pinnacle above its roof.
  2. ^ The Akṣobhya statue is dressed in lhegā.
  3. ^ Previously, a caitya with a gilded Buddha (suvarṇa Buddha) statue was erected in the place where the Dharmadhātujinālaṃkṛta Caitya has been erected now. At present, no one knows whereabouts of this caitya. It is believed that this Bāhāḥ was named Suvarṇapura Mahāvirā because of this gilded Buddha statue.
  4. ^ This document mentions a dispute from NS 656 (1536 CE) between the members of Sum Bāhāḥ and their neighbor Phyāku Mulmī.
  5. ^ Twenty ropanīs of land belonging to the Bāhāḥ was returned to the Bāhāḥ’s guṭhī in 1862.
_source.displayname: Sum Bāhāḥ (before 1536 CE) || सुम् बाहा: ।। LAL2530

This Caitya is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) and exhibits a hybrid design. The bottom half features elements typical of a jvālāvali caitya such as lions at the corners of its base and a lotus pedastal, while the upper half resembles a śikharakūṭa caitya with its Lokeśvara statues and four Buddhas attached to the dome. The Caitya is in a good condition and has been cleaned recently.

The inscription of the Caitya mentions that its construction was funded by Nararāja Pāneju in 1944 CE. Nararāja also established a guṭhī to perform the daily and anniversary ritual worship of the Caitya. However, his descendants sold their property and moved away from the locality, selling the guṭhī land and thus bringing an end to the daily worship. The Caitya's anniversary worship is performed on the full moon day of Āśvina.

Mūchẽ Āgama is located to the north of the Bahādur Śāha. The building can be accessed through a small door opening on the western boundary wall.

The Āgama was located at the south of a small courtyard facing north. The main entry door on the ground floor can be reached by climbing up on to a raised plinth guarded by two small stone lions. The main carved door is flanked by two small blind windows on either sides. A small secondary entry door on the principal façade (the eastern end of the building) leads to a stairway. There were two three-fold pasukā jhyāḥ on the first and second floor, both of which were salvaged after the earthquake.

The historical name of the Āgama is Maṇichẽ, meaning a house located in the Maṇigala Ṭola. The word maṇichẽ has changed into mūchẽ over the course of time. This building appears to be a normal residential building, however, this is in fact the āgãchẽ of the Jośīs of Bakhumbāhāla and Kisis (Śreṣṭha) of Ombāhāla. The Rājopādhyāyas of the Svãtha Ṭola perform the daily ritual worship here. Manamāneśvarī, the lineage deity of Licchavi kings who was worshipped before Taleju was brought to the Valley, is also worshipped inside this shrine.

The Āgama used to house a collection of the swords of kings. When a ruling king died, his sword was preserved here. Jośī (2065, 16-17) states that there were once more than 30 swords inside this Āgama. The three-storey building of the Āgama was heavily damaged in the 2015 earthquake and now only the front wall of the ground floor remains. The main deity has been relocated to a neighboring house and various small images have been preserved in the Patan Museum. 

No historical record confirming the initial construction of the shrine is available. A Gaṇeśa statue located to the north-west was established in 1434 (NS 558). This provides grounds to assume that the Āgama may also have been constructed around this time, or may even pre-date the statue.

Bhagavān Degaḥ is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001). It was originally built as a two-tiered temple and later converted into a hybrid structure with a domed roof. Bhagavān Degaḥ is partly depicted in a watercolour by Henry Ambrose Oldfield, dated 1857. This painting serves as the sole documentation of the temple’s restorations and reconfigurations over the past 150 years. No records of its initial construction could be found. It can be assumed that the temple was severely damaged in the 1934 earthquake and was later rebuilt in its current shape. The lower roof was preserved but the upper roof was replaced by a plastered brick dome with a gilt copper finial. Later, the lower roof was rebuilt with a brass sheet cover and decorative eaves. The original open pillar arcade was closed off with lattice woodwork and a door was installed in the east façade. This work was probably carried out some time between 1980-1990. The inner cella was partly covered with industrial tiles and a new door and a steel scissor gate have also been installed for security purposes. Today, only a few of the original components survive; these include the carved pillars, corbels and cross beams. Most of the edge stones and original tile floors have been lost.

Until a few decades ago this temple was known as the Sṛṣṭikāntā Lokeśvara Temple. Even the 2002 book Cultural Heritage of Bungmati (in p. 53) refers to it as the temple of Sṛṣṭikāntā Lokeśvara. A statue of Śākyamuni Buddha was enshrined in this temple around four decades ago. Before this, the sanctum of the temple was empty. The temple's new name of Bhagavān Degaḥ is closely related to this new deity.  

Elderly people in Bungmati tell of a legend which links this temple with the Sṛṣṭikāntā Lokeśvara Temple of Nālā (in the Kabhrepalnacok district). According to this story, the idol of Sṛṣṭikāntā Lokeśvara (which is currently in Nālā) was originally to be found in this temple. Some time ago, the idol disappeared from the temple of Bungmati. Eventually, it was found lying in the mud somewhere. ‘Nāla’ is a Newari word meaning mud. The deity found in the ‘nāla’ was then established in its current location.

Only the Pāneju Saṅgha of Bungmati have the right to perform the life-cycle (daśakarma) rites of Sṛṣṭikāntā Lokeśvara in Nālā. A group of eight pānejus from Bungmati goes to Nālā for this purpose every year on the full moon day of Phāguna. Like the temple of Nālā, this temple also faces east.

Since the Buddha statue was established in the temple, two families of Śākyas and Tulādhara have taken on responsibility for performing the ritual worships. A procession now also takes place in Bungmati on the day of Buddha Jayantī (the full moon day of Vaiśākha). On this day, people place the deity on a cot and carry him around the surrounding area of Bungmati.

According to this story, the idol of Sṛṣṭikāntā Lokeśvara (which is currently in Nālā) was originally to be found in this temple. Some time ago, the idol disappeared from the temple of Bungmati. Eventually, it was found lying in the mud somewhere. ‘Nāla’ is a Newari word meaning mud. The deity found in the ‘nāla’ was then established in its current location.

Only the Pāneju Saṅgha of Bungmati have the right to perform the life-cycle (daśakarma) rites of Sṛṣṭikāntā Lokeśvara in Nālā. A group of eight pānejus from Bungmati goes to Nālā for this purpose every year on the full moon day of Phāguna. Like the temple of Nālā, this temple also faces east.

Since the Buddha statue was established in the temple, two families of Śākyas and Tulādhara have taken on responsibility for performing the ritual worships. A procession now also takes place in Bungmati on the day of Buddha Jayantī (the full moon day of Vaiśākha). On this day, people place the deity on a cot and carry him around the surrounding area of Bungmati.

Gaṇeśa Mandira is located in Kotā Ṭola, Bungmati. The Tulādhara and Mālī caste groups worship this Gaṇeśa as their local deity. The mandira faces south and has a jhĩgaṭī tiled roof supported by carved struts. A metal pinnacle and parasol can be found atop the roof. A toraṇa has been placed above the carved wooden door. The main façade is decorated with latticed woodwork and two small latticed windows have been installed in the eastern and western walls of the temple.

An aniconic stone image of Gaṇeśa with a metal crown on his head is enshrined in the sanctum. Besides the main shrine, many iconic and aniconic stone images can be seen around the sanctum. A wooden toraṇa is attached to the eastern wall. There was a hiti (stepwell) to the east of the temple until a few decades ago. However, it gradually turned into a rubbish dumping site and was eventually covered up with mud. Before the hiti was completely filled in, some of the statues were removed and relocated to this temple and the nearby Licchavi caitya (BUN0026).

The temple was reconstructed in 2003. The projecting roof on the northern side was left unfinished during the reconstruction process, meaning that the temple's structure appears unbalanced. Local residents traditionally come to this temple to worship Gaṇeśa before they begin any other auspicious rituals such as initiation ceremonies, marriage or jaṃko (Skt. bhīmarathārohaṇa). The Kusle (Kapālī) community were responsible for taking care of this temple until a few years ago. However, now that this community no longer takes care of this temple there are no official caretakers (dyaḥpāḥlāḥs).
